questions.question: Explain the bargaining imbalance labour law answers, the constitutional rights held by each side, and the three principles running through the LRA.
questions.expected_answer: A lone job-seeker bargains from weakness: the firm can outlast a vacancy while the applicant cannot outlast hunger, and where many want one post, a single objection to the terms is meaningless — the unregulated industrial age showed the result. The Constitution guarantees fair labour practices and the rights to form and join unions, to organise, to bargain collectively and to strike; employers hold mirror rights to form employers' organisations and, within the law, to lock out. The LRA's principles: self-government — the organised parties negotiate their own terms while the state builds the arena but does not dictate the wage; majoritarianism — the majority union becomes the recognised voice with organisational rights, one strong voice rather than fragments; consultation — employers must consult and disclose before decisions that land on workers, retrenchment above all.

questions.question: Match the three statutes to their jobs with provisions from each, and distinguish the collective bargaining institutions by level and function.
questions.expected_answer: LRA — rules of engagement: union organisational rights, bargaining councils and workplace forums, protected strikes and lock-outs with their procedures, unfair dismissal protection, and the CCMA and Labour Courts. BCEA — the floor beneath every contract: maximum hours and overtime multipliers, minimum leave (annual, sick, family responsibility, maternity), meal and rest breaks, notice periods, and bans on child and forced labour — improvable by contract, never lowerable. COIDA — the safety net: claims against an employer-financed state fund for injury or occupational disease (medical costs, disability, dependants' benefits), no lawsuit or proof of negligence required, employers shielded from individual claims in exchange. Institutions: unions recruit, represent and negotiate; employers' organisations mirror them; bargaining councils convene permanent sector-level negotiation, with agreements extendable across the whole sector; workplace forums, elected by all workers of one large workplace, consult on workplace change — consultation, not wage bargaining.

questions.question: Separate conciliation, mediation and arbitration by who decides; place the labour courts; and explain when a strike is protected.
questions.expected_answer: At the CCMA — statutory, independent and free — conciliation has a commissioner steer the parties toward their own settlement, deciding nothing; mediation adds actively proposed solutions the parties may still refuse; arbitration has the commissioner hear evidence and issue a binding award. The ladder is ordered so self-built agreements come before imposed outcomes, and most disputes settle on the lowest rung. Above the CCMA stand the Labour Court — reviewing awards, interpreting the statutes, ruling on strikes and retrenchments — and the Labour Appeal Court. A strike is protected when the procedures were honoured (dispute referred, notice delivered), shielding strikers from dismissal for striking; skipping the procedures leaves the strike unprotected and its strikers without that shield.
